2. The relevant facts for the disposal of the appeal, in short, are that the appellants instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of their title in the suit covering an area of 1.20 acres of C.S. Plot No. 1 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 53 of Mouza Kakrail., Police Station Ramna, (former Keranigonj) Dhaka alleging, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands measuring 48.90 acres of said Plot and Khatian corresponding to S.A. Plot No.64 and S.A. Khatian No. 26 originally belonged to Bhawal Zaminder Rajkumer Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury who settled the suit land to Ashraf Ali Kazi, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs executing a pattannama on 05.02.1905. Said Ashraf Ali Kazi took over possession of the suit land and paid rent to the Zaminder. In C.S. operation, the suit land along with other lands of the disputed jam, was recorded in the name of Public Works Department under Bharat Samrat. Against the said record of right Ashraf Ali Kazi filed objection to get the same corrected and got an order on 24.05.1925. In S.A. operation the same was again recorded in the name of Public Works Department. On 12.01.1992, the plaintiffs discovered the pattannama, rent receipts and mutated C.S. Khatian in an old box in their house. On 08.03.1992, they collected the certified copies of the S.A. and C.S. Khatians and confirmed about the erroneous preparation of S.A. record of right. Thereafter, they filed this suit. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider the sub-missions of the appellants that the plaintiffs having proved their permanent settlement of the year 1905 producing pattanama (Ext.1) and the rent receipts of the years 1907, 1912, 1928, 1932, 1938, 1940, 1945 and 1948 (Exhibit-2 series proved their title in the suit land as well as their uninterrupted possession in the same over 87 years, the third Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in dismissing the suit. The Second submission was that the pattannama (exhibit-1) written in the year 1905 on stamp paper of more than 30 years old and the value of the land was shown at 11.15/- only and in such view of the matter, the same was not required to be registered under Section 17 of the Registration Act. The next point was that the plaintiffs' predecessor Ashraf Ali Kazi paid rents to the landlord vide exhibit-2 series are the best piece of evidence of possession of the plaintiffs in .the suit land. It was further pointed out that the C.S. record of right stand corrected on the basis of the objection filed by Ashraf Ali Kazi (exhibit-3 series). It was further pointed out that the documents produced by the plaintiffs were old documents of more than 30 years so as per provision of section 90 of the Evidence Act those documents should be accepted as legal evidence. 

 6. Mr. A.F. Hasan Arif, the senior Counsel 'appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff-appellants got the suit land by way of settlement in the year 1905 and produced more than 30 years old pattannama (exhibit-1) . The plaintiffs paid rents to the Zaminder vide Exhibit-2 series and they got the C.S. Khatian corrected vide exhibit-3 series and had been possessing the suit land more than 87 years. The third Judge of the High Court Division has committed an error of law in disbelieving the pattannama, corrected C.S. Khatian and rent receipts. He submits that the findings of the third Judge of the High Court Division regarding authenticity of exhibit-1 made in an old British Indian Stamp of 1905, and the rent receipts (exhib-it-2 series), the corrected C.S. Khatian (exhibit 3 series) and exhibit-4, the volume book of Government containing C.S. Khatian are erroneous. He further submits that since price of the land was Tk. 15/- only as it appears in the pattannama, the same was not required to he registered under section 17 of the Registration Act. 

 7. Mr. Goutom Kumar, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the High Court Division on vivid discussions on the materials on record came to the conclusion that the pattannama, rent receipts of the Zamindar and corrected C.S. Khatian are forged and fabricated documents. He submits that Mr. Justice Md. Abdur Rashid rightly directed to prosecute the plaintiff-appellants initiating proceeding under Section 476 read with 195 (1) (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on allegation of forging those documents. He submits that the plaintiffs had no title-and possession in the suit land. The Government, constructing the buildings in the suit land; has been possessing the same. The instant suit was not at all maintainable without the prayer for recovery of khas possession. 

 9. The case of the plaintiffs is that their predecessor Ashraf Ali Kazi took settlement of the suit land on the basis of pattannama dated 05.02.1995 (exhibit-i). P.W.1 Abdul Matin Kazi, who was about 67 years old at the time of adducing his evidence on 19.08.1994 (that is, he was born after 22 years of alleged execution of the said pattannama) in his evidence, inter alia, said, এই সেই পত্তন নামার মূল কপি প্রঃ- ১ হিসাবে চিহ্নিত। কোর্ট দাখিল করিলাম। বিবাদীপক্ষে এই মর্মে আপত্তি যে, লেখা অষ্পষ্ট ও ছেড়া প্রঃ ১টি। নোটারি পাবলিক কর্তৃক প্রত্তন নামার সত্যায়িত টাইপ কপি দাখিল করিলাম। প্রঃ ১(ক) আপত্তি সহকারে”। The is, exhibit-1 and 1(Ka) had been admitted in evidence with objection. The plaintiffs examined P.W.2 Sailendra Nath Sarker, a man of 78 years old, to prove the pattannama. In his cross-examination he said " ১নং প্রদর্শনী পড়তে পারব না।" From his evidence it appears that this witness was horn sometime in 1916, that is, after 11 years of the alleged execution of the pattannama. In order to substantiate the contents of the pattannama, the plaintiffs produced a notarized copy of the said pattannama exhibit-1(ka) P.W. 2 admitted that contents of the exhibit-1 are not readable. The plaintiffs did not examine the writer of the duplicated pattannama nor they examined the notary public, who notarized the same. In such view of the matter, Ext.1(Ka) could not be relied on. In the case of Harihar Prashad Vs. Desnarain reported in AIR 1956 SC 305 it was observed that the presumption enacted in Section 90 of the Evidence Act can be raised only with reference to original documents not to copies thereof. Furthermore, it appears that from Ext.1(Ka) that Ext.1 had been executed by Sree Kamini Kumar Bandapadhya on behalf of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury. The P.W. 2, who claimed to be the Tahsilder of Bhawal Estate and joined in the said Estate in 1346 B.S., did not say in his evidence that Sree Kamini Kumar Bandapadhya was the Manager of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, the Zaminder of Bhawal Estate. The plaintiffs failed to produce any other evidence to prove that Kamini Kumar Bandapadhya was the manager of the Estate. 

 10. Submission of Mr. Arif is that since the Ext. 1 Pattannama is an old document of more than 30 years and had been produced from proper custody, the court would presume that the signature and every other part of Ext.1 is that person's hand writing and, the same had been duly executed by the person by whom it purports to be executed as per provision of Section 90 of the Evidence Act. The spirit of section 90 of the Evidence Act is that if private documents not less than thirty years old are produced from proper custody and are on their face free from suspicion, the court may presume at they w have been signed or written by the persons whose signatures they bear or in whose hand writing they purport to he, that they have been duly attested and executed, if they purport so to he Section 90 only lays down that the court may presume that document purporting to be 30 years old are genuine. That it must not presume them to be so. Supreme Court of India in the case of Sri Lakhi Baruah Vs. Sri Padma Kanta Kalita reported in AIR 1996 SC 1253 observed that Section 90 of the Evidence Act is founded on necessity and convenience because it is extremely difficult and sometimes not possible to lead evidence to prove handwriting, signature or execution of old documents after lapse of 30 years. In order to obviate such difficulties or improbabilities to prove execution of an old documents section 30 has been incorporated in the Evidence Act, which does away with the strict rule of proof of private documents. Presumption of genuineness may he raised if the document in question is produced from proper custody. It is, however, the discretion of the Court to accept the presumption flowing from Section. The presumption is permissive and accordance no the circumstances of each case the court may or may not raise it. That is, such presumption discretionary and so where a document is suspicious on the face of it or mutilated, the court may refuse to make presumption. It is not obligatory on a court to raise the presumption. The language being "may" when the person who has been examined as P.W.2 to prove the Ext.1 himself has said “১নং প্রদর্শনী পড়তে পারবো না"; then why the court will rely upon such document .At the time of making exhibit the defendant raised objection saving, লেখা অষ্পষ্ট ও ছেড়া প্রঃ ১টি। In such circumstances, the provision of section 90 ought to be applied with more care and great caution because nothing can he more easy than, for an unscrupulous ours person, who is wrongfully in possession and wants to make out a title to it to forge such document in his favour more than 30 years old and produce it as the proper custodian relieving himself of the necessity of proving its execution. The Ext. 1 patina must not be presumed to he genuine merely from its being ancient. Some other evidence were required to be given of the early existence and publicity of Ext. 1 . Neither C. S. khatian nor S. A. khatian had been prepared on the basis of Ext. 1. 

 17. A controversy has arisen as to whether the instant permanent tenancy can be created otherwise by a registered instrument. The last court of facts held that the suit land is non- agriculture land to be used for non-agricultural purpose. The Contents of pattanipatta or amalnama as reproduced in duplicatted copy (Ext 1Ka) were as follows: 

 18. From the contents of Ext. 1(Ka), intention of the parties as gathered from those contents; surrounding circumstances and the claim of the plaintiffs it appears to us that the plaintiffs tried to establish that the Ext. 1 is a lease deed which is unregistered and unilateral one in respect of the property described therein and which is to be used for orchard and homestead and the same is a lease in perpetuity. In the case of Safar Ali Master Vs. Abdul Mazid reported in 47 CLJ Page 27 it was observed that homestead land within a municipality even, though recorded as "bagan" land in the record of rights is not governed by the Bengol Tenancy Act but by the Transfer of Property Act. In the case of Ramdas Vs. Bipradas reported in 19 C.W.N. page 35 it was held that tenancies for residential purposes are outside the scope of the Bengol Tenancy Act. We are of the view that the alleged iv lease was to be regulated under the provision of Transfer of Property Act not by the Bengol Tenancy Act. Lease as defined in section 105 of the transfer of Property Act is a transfer of right to enjoy immovable property made for a certain time express or implied, or in perpetuity. In the case of Abdus Satter Vs. Suresh Chandra Das reported in 32 DLR (AD) page 170 it has been observed that the essential elements constituting lease are the following: a) the right must be one as to immovable property, (b) the right must be that enjoyment of immovable property; (c) these must be a transfer of much right; (d) the right of transfer must be made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity; (f) the consideration must be of the particular kind namely, premium or rent as defined by the section either or both of them. In the case of M.H. Khondker, Advocate Vs. Bangladesh reported in 30 DLR (SC)1 it has been held that (i) by a lease a subordinate interest is created by a person in favour of another person in respect of some immovable property on condition of premium or rent (ii) the right which is created a lease is the right of tenancy 'Lease" and tenancy are cognate terms, implying the same kind of jural relationship. In the case of Bastacolla Colliery Co. Ltd. Vs. Bandhu Beldar reported AIR 1960 Pat 344 it has been observed by the Full Bench of Patna High Court that before amendment of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act by Act 20 of 1929 a valid lease could be created by a patta executed by the lessor but all leases coming within the first paragraph of Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act can only be made by registered instrument. Since the instant transaction is a transfer of interest of non- agricultural land and to be used for nonagricultural purpose entitling the leasee the enjoyment of such immovable property which includes the right to possession thereof in perpetuity such tenancy can only be created by registered instrument. An unregistered documents of lease which was required to be registered conveyed no title and created no right of the plaintiffs. Ext. 1 is inoperative under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and could not create a tenancy; could not create the inception of tenancy and could not be considered to find out tenancy. A document which was compulsorily registrable but was not registered is void as regards immovable property which is non agriculture in nature and to be used for non-agricultural purposes.
